key_findings.title: Monocular Depth Estimation: A Survey
key_findings.summary: Comprehensive overview of traditional vs. deep‑learning approaches, covering supervised, self‑supervised, and semi‑supervised paradigms, benchmark datasets, metrics, challenges and future directions.

key_findings.title: How Attention Boosts Monocular Depth Estimation: A Survey
key_findings.summary: Focuses on the impact of attention mechanisms (self‑attention, cross‑attention, transformer encoders) on depth prediction accuracy, efficiency, and ability to capture long‑range context.

key_findings.title: Survey on unsupervised monocular depth estimation in dynamic scenes based on deep learning
key_findings.summary: Analyzes unsupervised/self‑supervised methods that handle moving objects and dynamic illumination, discusses motion segmentation, optical‑flow integration, and robustness to real‑world driving scenarios.

key_findings.title: Review of monocular depth estimation methods
key_findings.summary: Covers both classic geometry‑based pipelines and modern deep neural networks, evaluates metric vs. relative depth, and outlines open problems such as domain shift and real‑time deployment.

key_findings.title: Survey on Monocular Metric Depth Estimation
key_findings.summary: Dedicated to absolute‑scale depth prediction, discusses dataset requirements, scale‑consistent loss designs, multi‑task learning (e.g., depth + pose), and applications in SLAM and AR.

key_findings.title: A Survey of the State of the Art in Monocular 3D Human Pose Estimation: Methods, Benchmarks, and Challenges
key_findings.summary: While centered on human pose, the paper provides a valuable discussion of depth ambiguity in single‑view settings and surveys diffusion and state‑space models that are increasingly adopted for depth‑aware pose estimation.

key_findings.title: A Survey of Self‑Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation Based on Deep Neural Networks
key_findings.summary: Classifies 89 self‑supervised works, reviews photometric, reprojection, and semantic consistency losses, and highlights emerging trends such as multi‑modal self‑supervision and video‑level training.

key_findings.title: Towards Depth Foundation Model: Recent Trends in Vision‑Based Depth Estimation
key_findings.summary: Proposes the concept of a depth foundation model trained on massive multi‑domain data, surveys scaling laws, large‑scale architecture (ViT‑G, Swin‑V2), and zero‑shot generalization across monocular, stereo, and video settings.

synthesis:
The period 2023‑2026 marks a consolidation and rapid expansion of monocular depth estimation research. Early 2023 surveys laid out the classic taxonomy (traditional geometry vs. deep learning) and highlighted the emergence of attention‑based transformers. By 2023‑2024, the community shifted toward self‑supervised and unsupervised learning to bypass costly depth sensors, with a strong emphasis on handling dynamic scenes (moving objects, varying illumination) through motion segmentation and video‑level photometric constraints. 

Metric depth estimation gained prominence as applications (AR/VR, robotics, SLAM) demanded absolute scale; dedicated surveys in 2025 dissected scale‑consistent loss functions, multi‑task frameworks (depth+pose+semantic), and the role of high‑quality metric datasets (KITTI, NYU‑Depth v2, TartanAir, ApolloScape). Concurrently, attention mechanisms—originally popular in NLP—became a core component of state‑of‑the‑art models, improving long‑range context capture and enabling high‑resolution predictions with less memory via hierarchical transformers.

A noteworthy trend is the inception of "depth foundation models" (2025). Inspired by large language and vision models, researchers are training massive vision transformers on billions of images paired with sparse depth, synthetic data, or multi‑view geometry, achieving zero‑shot generalization to unseen domains and sensor configurations. This direction promises to alleviate the domain‑gap problem that has long plagued monocular depth methods.

Across all surveys, several recurring challenges are identified: (1) domain shift between indoor/outdoor or synthetic/real data; (2) preserving fine‑grained structural details while maintaining real‑time inference; (3) robust depth estimation under dynamic motion; and (4) reliable metric scaling without external sensors. Proposed solutions include domain‑adaptive training (style‑transfer, test‑time adaptation), hybrid CNN‑Transformer backbones, diffusion‑based depth refinement, and integration of semantic priors from large‑scale vision‑language models.

In summary, the 2023‑2026 literature illustrates a clear trajectory: from supervised, relatively shallow CNNs toward self‑supervised, transformer‑centric, and foundation‑model approaches that aim for universal, metric‑accurate depth prediction usable across robotics, autonomous driving, and immersive media. Future work is expected to converge on large‑scale pre‑training, multimodal self‑supervision, and real‑time deployment on edge devices, closing the gap between research prototypes and production systems.
